newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Major pins election hopes on economy.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Major pins election hopes on economy.

text.p: "It's the economy, stupid!"

This celebrated line helped Bill Clinton win the U.S. presidency in 1992 and now John Major hopes the same focus on the economy can rescue his fading chances of winning a new term as British prime minister.

Worn down by divisions in his Conservative Party over Europe and shorn of his majority in parliament, Major is running out of time to overhaul the opposition Labour Party's poll lead of more than 20 percentage points. The election must be held by May 22.
The task looks forlorn, but Major is convinced that what he calls Britain's Rolls-Royce recovery will give the Conservatives a fighting chance of winning a fifth consecutive term of office.

"No government will ever have gone into a general election since the Second World War with the economy in such good shape, with the prospects for the future in such good order as they are at the moment," Major said in a recent interview.
"And upon that record and what we can do with it for the British nation in the future we will base our appeal at the general election," he said.

Unemployment has fallen below two million for the first time in six years, take-home pay is rising at the fastest rate since the boom years of the 1980s and house prices -- critical in a country where most people own their homes -- are on the way up.
As the Guardian commented: "If robust economies always won elections then the Conservatives would be half way home by now instead of trailing hopelessly in the polls."

Instead, the paper said, voters feel they have been deceived too often to take good news at face value. They also realise the seeds for the recovery were sown by the collapse of a central plank of government policy, when sterling was ignominiously ejected from Europe's exchange rate mechanism (ERM) in 1992.
The government's mishandling of issues such as mad cow disease and a clumsy attempt to pad its majority in a recent fishing vote have also overshadowed Major's economic record.

"Against this background, it is all but impossible for his main campaigning message -- that the UK has entered the most virtuous phase in the economic cycle for decades -- to get through," Financial Times political editor Robert Preston wrote.
Several political economists believe that the link between economic recovery and the government's political fortunes snapped when Major was forced to leave the ERM in 1992.
"When a government falls flat on its face as this one did then, the dynamics are against it," Professor Peter Spencer of London's Birkbeck College said.
"Once a government has lost its reputation for competence, other things follow.".

But Michael Dicks, an economist with investment bank Lehman Brothers, believes the drop in government support after the ERM debacle was in fact due to a sharp rise at the same time in "negative equity" -- the extent to which a homeowner's mortgage debt exceeds the value of his house.
Now that house prices are rising briskly, negative equity is melting away and Dicks expects a rapid recovery in the Conservatives' poll ratings as a result.

By May, the race could be very tight. "Although a Labour victory still looks like the most probable outcome, there are significant risks of either no party winning a majority or of the Labour "victory' being a hollow one -- in the sense of its resulting in only a tiny majority," Dicks said.
But one ministerial adviser, who has devised his own statistical model of the political impact of economic trends, believes Major has left it too late.
The official dismissed the theory that ejection from the ERM had irreparably damaged the government's credibility.

But he said the harm done by feuding over Europe, and the clamour for change after nearly 18 years of Conservative rule, meant Major would have needed another year of good economic news before he stood a fighting chance at the ballot box.
"This time round it really isn't the economy, stupid," he said.
